documents.title: Helen Marsh, glaciologist who read the history of the climate in ice, dies at 84
paragraphs: Helen Marsh, the glaciologist whose pioneering work on Antarctic ice cores changed how scientists understand the climate of the past, died on Tuesday at her home in Cambridge. She was 84. The cause was heart failure, her family said.

She was born in 1941 in a mining town in the north of England, the second of four children. Her father worked underground; her mother took in sewing. Neither had studied beyond the age of fourteen, yet both insisted that their daughter would. A scholarship took her to Durham, where she was the only woman in her year to study physics.

It was in Antarctica, in the winter of 1974, that she made the discovery for which she is remembered. Drilling through two kilometres of ice, her team recovered a core that held tiny bubbles of air, each one a sample of the atmosphere as it had been many thousands of years earlier. Marsh was the first to see that these bubbles could be read like the pages of a book. Her tireless, almost stubborn insistence on checking every measurement twice turned a curiosity into a method.

Colleagues remember a scientist who could not be hurried and could not be flattered. Dr Samir Haddad, who worked beside her for thirty years, recalled that she once sent back a prize committee’s draft citation because it called her work “brilliant”. “She said the word was lazy,” he said. “She wanted them to say what the work had actually shown.”

Away from the laboratory, she was, by all accounts, a very different person: noisy, generous and hopeless at keeping a schedule. She married the geologist Peter Lindqvist in 1968, and their kitchen in Cambridge became an informal meeting place for students far from home. Her daughter, Anna, remembers dinners at which a discussion of carbon dioxide would give way, without warning, to an argument about football.

The two sides of her life were never as separate as she liked to pretend. When her husband fell ill in 1991, she turned down a chair at a university in California so that she could stay and look after him. She returned to full-time research only after his death, six years later, and often said that those years had taught her more about patience than any glacier.

Honours came late and she accepted them with visible discomfort. She was an unassuming woman who wore the same grey cardigan to a ceremony at the Royal Society as she wore to feed the birds, and she joked that the medal would “look better on someone with a better coat”. She never sought publicity, and gave most of her prize money to a fund for students from mining towns.

Marsh is survived by her daughter, Anna, and two grandchildren. In a tribute issued yesterday, the university said that her death marked the end of an era, but that the method she gave science would outlast it.

documents.title: Arthur Penhallow, botanist who saved a thousand varieties of apple, dies at 91
paragraphs: Arthur Penhallow, who spent six decades collecting and cataloguing the old apple varieties of south-west England, died on Sunday in a nursing home in Truro. He was 91.

In the 1950s, when farmers were grubbing up their orchards to plant more profitable crops, Penhallow began visiting them on a bicycle, asking to take cuttings from trees that were about to be felled. Many of the varieties he rescued, with names such as Cornish Blush and Penrose Sweet, existed nowhere else. By 1980 his collection at Polwyn held more than a thousand.

He was not an easy man. Former assistants describe a scholar who corrected their spelling in front of visitors and who regarded the telephone as an intrusion. He fell out with the county council, two universities and, for a decade, his own brother, over a disagreement about the correct name of a single tree. Few of those who worked with him would have called him warm.

Yet the same people speak of him with a respect that is close to awe. Every autumn he posted a box of fruit to each of the farmers he had visited, and he kept up the habit long after most of them had died, sending the boxes to their grandchildren instead. He never married. His correspondence, now in the county archive, runs to some four thousand letters, almost all of them about apples.

items.question: Why has this text been written?

options.text: To announce a new scientific discovery
To mark a death and honour a life
To advertise a university course
To explain how ice cores are drilled

answerExplanation.en: It opens with her death at 84 and then tells the story of her life: that is what an obituary does. The discovery is part of the story, not its news.
answerExplanation.fr: Le texte s’ouvre sur sa mort à 84 ans puis raconte sa vie : c’est le rôle d’une nécrologie. La découverte fait partie du récit, ce n’en est pas la nouvelle.
answerExplanation.de: Der Text beginnt mit ihrem Tod mit 84 und erzählt dann ihr Leben: Das ist die Aufgabe eines Nachrufs. Die Entdeckung gehört zur Geschichte, sie ist nicht die Neuigkeit.

items.question: What did Marsh’s team discover in Antarctica?

options.text: Air bubbles in ice preserve samples of the ancient atmosphere
A glacier that was growing instead of shrinking
A way of forecasting next winter’s weather
A new route across the ice

answerExplanation.en: The core held tiny bubbles, each a sample of the atmosphere from thousands of years earlier, which could be “read like the pages of a book”.
answerExplanation.fr: La carotte contenait de minuscules bulles, chacune un échantillon de l’atmosphère d’il y a des milliers d’années, qu’on pouvait « lire comme les pages d’un livre ».
answerExplanation.de: Der Kern enthielt winzige Bläschen, jedes eine Probe der Atmosphäre von vor Tausenden von Jahren, die man „wie die Seiten eines Buches lesen“ konnte.

items.question: Why did Marsh turn down the chair in California?

options.text: She disliked the climate there
She wanted to stay and look after her husband
The university offered her too little money
She had decided to stop doing research

answerExplanation.en: “So that she could stay and look after him”: her husband was ill. She went back to full-time research only after his death.
answerExplanation.fr: « So that she could stay and look after him » : son mari était malade. Elle n’a repris la recherche à plein temps qu’après sa mort.
answerExplanation.de: „So that she could stay and look after him“: Ihr Mann war krank. Erst nach seinem Tod kehrte sie zur Vollzeitforschung zurück.

items.statement: Marsh was delighted when a prize committee described her work as “brilliant”.

answerExplanation.en: False: she sent the draft back, saying the word was lazy and that she wanted them to say what the work had actually shown.
answerExplanation.fr: Faux : elle a renvoyé le texte en disant que le mot était paresseux et qu’elle voulait qu’on dise ce que le travail avait réellement montré.
answerExplanation.de: Falsch: Sie schickte den Entwurf zurück, weil das Wort faul sei und sie wollte, dass man sagt, was die Arbeit tatsächlich gezeigt hatte.

items.question: What does the tone of the obituary suggest about the writer’s view of Marsh?

options.text: She admires and is fond of Marsh, and smiles at her little oddities
She respects Marsh’s work but finds her cold and distant
She is critical of Marsh for refusing praise
She has no opinion and simply lists the facts

answerExplanation.en: Details such as “hopeless at keeping a schedule”, the grey cardigan and the joke about the coat are gently humorous. The writer clearly admires and likes her.
answerExplanation.fr: Des détails comme « hopeless at keeping a schedule », le gilet gris et la plaisanterie sur le manteau sont d’un humour doux. L’auteur l’admire et l’apprécie clairement.
answerExplanation.de: Details wie „hopeless at keeping a schedule“, die graue Strickjacke und der Witz über den Mantel sind sanft humorvoll. Die Autorin bewundert und mag sie offensichtlich.

items.question: What does the detail of the boxes of fruit posted every autumn show?

options.text: That he was quietly generous and loyal
That he hoped to sell his collection

answerExplanation.en: He kept sending fruit for years, even to the grandchildren of farmers who had died. The writer uses it to show a kindness his manner hid.

answerExplanation.de: Er schickte jahrelang Obst, sogar an die Enkel verstorbener Bauern. Der Autor zeigt damit eine Güte, die sein Auftreten verbarg.

items.statement: Penhallow’s quarrel with his brother lasted about ten years.

answerExplanation.en: True: he fell out with his own brother “for a decade” over the name of a single tree.

answerExplanation.de: Richtig: Er überwarf sich „for a decade“ mit seinem Bruder wegen des Namens eines einzigen Baums.
